text: A sixty-five-year-old widow entered a Puerto Rico emergency room with chills, cold sweat, dizziness, and chest pains. At the desk, she received a number.
provenance: On the morning of the sixth of September, 1991, a sixty-five-year-old widow in Puerto Rico woke up feeling, in her son's words, real bad.

text: The hospital's position was precise: it had not denied her screening or treatment and would have attended to her if she had waited.
provenance: The hospital said it had neither denied Ms. Gonzalez an initial screening nor refused her essential treatment.

text: But the jury heard evidence that she arrived in critical condition and received what the court called only a high number and a cold shoulder.
provenance: A high number and a cold shoulder.

text: The court said a complete failure to attend someone showing symptoms widely understood as an acute threat can itself deny an appropriate screening.
provenance: Regardless of motive, the court wrote, a complete failure to attend a patient who presents a condition that practically everyone knows may indicate an immediate and acute threat to life can constitute a denial of an appropriate medical screening examination.

text: That is constructive refusal: nobody says no, yet the system never reaches the person standing inside it asking for care.
provenance: Its point was that it gave the patient a number, and would have ministered to her had she waited.

text: This Short does not claim that the wait caused her death. The legal finding here concerns what happened while she waited.
provenance: It plays no part in what this case decided.

text: EMTALA promises a screening procedure administered even-handedly, not perfect treatment and not a guarantee that every patient is seen simultaneously.
The case began with a number handed across a desk, and it ends with the same number still waiting to be called.
provenance: A high number and a cold shoulder.
